items.prose: Let $U = \{1, 2, \dots, 40\}$. In $U$, let $A$ be the set of multiples of 4 and $B$ the set of multiples of 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite. List the multiples of 4 up to 40, or divide 40 by 4.

byKey.no-forty: You left out 40. It is in $U$ and it is a multiple of 4, so $|A| = 10$.

explain.text: The multiples of 4 in $U$ are $4 \times 1$ up to $4 \times 10 = 40$. So $|A| = 10$.

feedback.correct: A number is in both when it is a multiple of 12: $A \cap B = \{12, 24, 36\}$, so $|A \cap B| = 3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the smallest number in both sets, then list its multiples up to 40.

byKey.product: You used multiples of $4 \times 6 = 24$. 12 is already a multiple of both, so the common elements are 12, 24 and 36.
byKey.all-b: 6 is $|B|$. Not every multiple of 6 is a multiple of 4: 6, 18 and 30 are not.

explain.text: An element of $A \cap B$ is a multiple of 4 and of 6, so a multiple of 12. In $U$ those are 12, 24 and 36, so $|A \cap B| = 3$.

parts.question: Using $|A \cap B| = 3$ from part 2, how many subsets does $A \cap B$ have?

feedback.correct: Each of the 3 elements is in or out, so there are $2^3 = 8$ subsets.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each element is either in a subset or out of it, independently.

byKey.times-two: You multiplied $2 \times 3$. Each element doubles the count, so it is $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$.
byKey.no-empty: You left out $\varnothing$. The empty set is a subset of every set, so there are 8.

explain.text: A subset is fixed by choosing in or out for each of the 3 elements, so there are $2^3 = 8$. The list runs from $\varnothing$ to $\{12, 24, 36\}$, and both count.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the sizes, then correct for the elements counted twice.

byKey.no-overlap: $10 + 6 = 16$ counts 12, 24 and 36 twice. Take off $|A \cap B| = 3$: 13.
byKey.added: You added the overlap instead of taking it away. It was counted twice already, so $10 + 6 - 3 = 13$.

explain.text: Adding $|A|$ and $|B|$ counts each element of $A \cap B$ twice. So $|A \cup B| = 10 + 6 - 3 = 13$.

parts.question: Using $|A \cup B| = 13$, how many elements of $U$ are in $A^c \cap B^c$?

feedback.correct: By De Morgan, $A^c \cap B^c = (A \cup B)^c$, so it has $40 - 13 = 27$ elements.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Rewrite $A^c \cap B^c$ with one of De Morgan's laws first.

byKey.carry-16: $40 - 16$ uses the union with the overlap counted twice. The union has 13 elements, so $40 - 13 = 27$.
byKey.wrong-law: $40 - 3 = 37$ counts $(A \cap B)^c$. De Morgan's law gives $A^c \cap B^c = (A \cup B)^c$, so take away 13: 27.

explain.text: A number is in neither set exactly when it is outside the union, so $A^c \cap B^c = (A \cup B)^c$. That set has $40 - 13 = 27$ elements.

items.prose: A scheduler sends each of 4 overnight jobs to one of 6 servers. An assignment is a function $f : J \to S$ from the set $J$ of jobs to the set $S$ of servers.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each pair is one job with one server.

byKey.added: You added $4 + 6$. A pair takes one job and one server, so there are $4 \times 6 = 24$.
byKey.functions: 1296 counts functions. $J \times S$ is the set of single pairs, and there are $4 \times 6 = 24$.

explain.text: Each element of $J \times S$ is a pair (job, server). There are 4 choices of job and 6 of server, so $4 \times 6 = 24$ pairs.

parts.question: A function is a set of pairs from $J \times S$ with exactly one pair for each job. How many functions $f : J \to S$ are there?

feedback.correct: Each of the 4 jobs picks one of 6 servers, so there are $6^4 = 1296$ functions.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each job picks a server on its own, and the choices multiply.

byKey.flipped: $4^6 = 4096$ counts functions from servers to jobs. Each of the 4 jobs has 6 choices: $6^4 = 1296$.
byKey.pairs: 24 is the number of pairs. A function picks 4 of them, one for each job: $6^4 = 1296$ ways.
byKey.one-to-one: 360 counts only assignments with no shared server. Two jobs may share, so it is $6^4 = 1296$.

explain.text: A function chooses one pair for each job, and each job has 6 servers to choose from. So there are $6 \times 6 \times 6 \times 6 = 1296$ functions.

parts.question: How many of the 1296 functions are one-to-one, with no server given two jobs?

feedback.correct: The jobs take 6, then 5, then 4, then 3 servers: $6 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3 = 360$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Once a server has a job, the next job cannot use it.

byKey.repeat: 1296 lets two jobs share a server. One-to-one takes a server away each time: $6 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3 = 360$.
byKey.unordered: 15 counts sets of 4 servers. The jobs are different, so each set can be handed out in 24 ways: $15 \times 24 = 360$.
byKey.jobs-only: $4! = 24$ orders the jobs. The servers run down from 6: $6 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3 = 360$.

explain.text: One-to-one means different jobs go to different servers. The first job has 6 servers, the next 5 left, then 4, then 3, so $6 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3 = 360$.

parts.question: Is any assignment $f : J \to S$ onto, with every server given a job?

options.text: No: 4 jobs can reach at most 4 of the 6 servers
Yes: every one-to-one assignment is also onto
options.why: One-to-one stops servers being shared, but 4 jobs still reach only 4 servers.

options.text: Yes: 1296 functions are far more than 6 servers
options.why: The count of functions says nothing about the servers each one reaches. Each has at most 4 outputs.

options.text: No: no function is both one-to-one and onto
options.why: A bijection is both. Here onto fails only because there are fewer jobs than servers.

feedback.correct: Right. The image has at most 4 elements, and $S$ has 6.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the outputs a single assignment can have.

explain.text: The image of $f$ holds at most one server per job, so at most 4 servers. $S$ has 6, so at least 2 servers are always left out and no assignment is onto.

parts.question: Using 1296 functions and 360 one-to-one ones, how many assignments give some server two or more jobs?

feedback.correct: Every assignment is one-to-one or not, so $1296 - 360 = 936$ share a server.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the complement: all functions minus the one-to-one ones.

byKey.added: You added the counts. The one-to-one ones are among the 1296, so take them away: $1296 - 360 = 936$.
byKey.carry-4096: You started from $4^6 = 4096$. There are $6^4 = 1296$ functions, so $1296 - 360 = 936$.

explain.text: An assignment that is not one-to-one gives some server two or more jobs. So the count is $1296 - 360 = 936$, which is most of the assignments.

parts.question: Which opening starts a proof that $f$ is one-to-one?

options.why: That holds for every function. One-to-one runs the other way: equal outputs force equal inputs.
One pair proves nothing about every pair. Start from any $a$ and $b$ with equal outputs.
That says different outputs come from different inputs, which every function satisfies.

feedback.correct: Right. Start from equal outputs and show the inputs are equal.
feedback.generic: Not quite. One-to-one says: if $f(a) = f(b)$, then $a = b$.

explain.text: One-to-one means $f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow a = b$, so the proof assumes equal outputs. From $9 - 3a = 9 - 3b$ we get $-3a = -3b$, so $a = b$.

parts.question: To show $f$ is onto, take any $y \in \mathbb{R}$. Which $x$ has $f(x) = y$? Write it in terms of $y$.

feedback.correct: From $9 - 3x = y$ we get $3x = 9 - y$, so $x = \tfrac{9 - y}{3}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Set $9 - 3x = y$ and solve for $x$.

byKey.sign: Check: $f\left(\tfrac{y - 9}{3}\right) = 9 - (y - 9) = 18 - y$, not $y$. Move $3x$ across: $3x = 9 - y$.
byKey.applied-f: You applied $f$ to $y$. We need the $x$ that $f$ sends to $y$: solve $9 - 3x = y$.
byKey.sign-y: Moving $y$ across changes its sign: $3x = 9 - y$, so $x = \tfrac{9 - y}{3}$.

explain.text: Solve $9 - 3x = y$: $3x = 9 - y$, so $x = \tfrac{9 - y}{3}$. Check: $f\left(\tfrac{9 - y}{3}\right) = 9 - (9 - y) = y$, so every real $y$ is reached.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $y = -6$ into $\tfrac{9 - y}{3}$, minding the two minus signs.

byKey.sign: You used $\tfrac{y - 9}{3}$. Check: $f(-5) = 24$, not $-6$. With $\tfrac{9 - y}{3}$ the answer is 5.
byKey.applied-f: 27 is $f(-6)$. The inverse asks which $x$ has $f(x) = -6$: $\tfrac{9 + 6}{3} = 5$.

parts.question: Now keep the rule but change the sets: $g : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ with $g(n) = 9 - 3n$. Using $n = \tfrac{9 - y}{3}$, how many of the integers from 1 to 30 are not in the image of $g$?

feedback.correct: $n = \tfrac{9 - y}{3}$ is an integer only when 3 divides $y$. From 1 to 30 that is 10 numbers, so $30 - 10 = 20$ are missed.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask for which $y$ the formula gives a whole number $n$.

byKey.hits: 10 is the number that are reached, the multiples of 3. The question asks for those missed: $30 - 10 = 20$.
byKey.onto: $f$ is onto $\mathbb{R}$, but $g$ must hit $y$ with a whole number. $y = 1$ needs $n = \tfrac{8}{3}$, so $g$ misses 20 of them.

explain.text: $g(n) = y$ needs $n = \tfrac{9 - y}{3}$ to be an integer, so 3 must divide $y$. From 1 to 30 there are 10 multiples of 3, so $30 - 10 = 20$ are missed. The same rule is onto with codomain $\mathbb{R}$ and not onto with $\mathbb{Z}$.

items.prose: Eight traders, numbered 1 to 8, sit two to a desk at four desks. Traders 1 and 2 sit at desk 1, 3 and 4 at desk 2, 5 and 6 at desk 3, and 7 and 8 at desk 4. Let $f$ send each trader to their desk, and for a set $X$ of traders let $f(X) = \{f(x) : x \in X\}$. The early shift is $A = \{1, 2, 3, 5\}$ and the late shift is $B = \{2, 4, 6, 7\}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Write down each trader's desk, then count the different desks.

byKey.traders: 4 counts traders. Traders 1 and 2 share desk 1, so $f(A) = \{1, 2, 3\}$ has 3 elements.

explain.text: $f(A)$ is the set of desks the early shift uses. Traders 1 and 2 share desk 1, and 3 and 5 sit at desks 2 and 3, so $f(A) = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $|f(A)| = 3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Intersect the two sets of desks as they stand.

byKey.image-of-meet: 1 is $|f(A \cap B)|$, which comes next. Here intersect the desks: $\{1, 2, 3\} \cap \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ has 3 elements.
byKey.union: 4 is the size of the union. The intersection keeps desks in both sets: $\{1, 2, 3\}$, so 3.

explain.text: Both shifts use desks 1, 2 and 3, and only the late shift uses desk 4. So $f(A) \cap f(B) = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and its size is 3.

parts.question: Now intersect the traders first. What is $|f(A \cap B)|$?

feedback.correct: $A \cap B = \{2\}$, so $f(A \cap B) = \{1\}$ and its size is 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the traders on both shifts, then their desks.

byKey.same: 3 is $|f(A) \cap f(B)|$ from part 2. Only trader 2 is on both shifts, so $f(A \cap B) = \{1\}$.
byKey.empty: Trader 2 is in both $A$ and $B$. So $A \cap B = \{2\}$ and $f(A \cap B) = \{1\}$ has 1 element.

explain.text: Only trader 2 works both shifts, so $A \cap B = \{2\}$ and $f(A \cap B) = \{1\}$, of size 1. That is smaller than the 3 of part 2.

parts.question: Parts 2 and 3 give 3 and 1. Which property of $f$, if it held, would force $f(A \cap B) = f(A) \cap f(B)$ for every $A$ and $B$?

options.text: One-to-one: no two traders share a desk
Onto: every desk has at least one trader
options.why: This $f$ is already onto, and the sets still differ. The gap comes from shared desks.

options.text: Equal shifts: $A$ and $B$ have the same size
options.why: Here both shifts have 4 traders and the sets still differ. Shared desks cause the gap.

options.text: A smaller codomain: fewer desks than traders
options.why: Fewer desks than traders is what forces sharing. That makes the gap more likely, not less.

feedback.correct: Right. With no shared desks, a desk reached from both shifts comes from one trader on both shifts.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at desks 2 and 3: how do both shifts reach them?

explain.text: Desks 2 and 3 are in both images through different traders, 3 and 4, then 5 and 6. If $f$ were one-to-one, a desk reached from $A$ and from $B$ would come from one trader, who would be in $A \cap B$.
